Alex.confusing: The Eagle's rule ("an egg for every visitor they had," where "they" is the target) confused me badly in round 1, and I wrongly pushed a false contradiction against Casey before retracting it.
Alex.fun: Round 1 as the Sphinx, where I learned who the Eagle was and got to steer the table's suspicion toward Casey while the rest of the table argued the egg math.
Alex.change: Publish each player's visit target and the animal's effect in a clearer way at dawn, so players don't misread role rules like the Eagle's.
Alex.regret: In round 3 I threw at Ellis based on my hug claim while Casey's story was clearly broken, and I should have gathered more evidence before committing to a throw that didn't match the eventual Meowfia pair.

Blair.confusing: The Eagle and Tit visit-count arithmetic: the Eagle counts visitors to its target, not to itself, and it took the whole table several beats to agree on that. Hug mechanics were also hard to pin down from the dawn reports alone.
Blair.fun: Round 2, when the table tangled over the hug and Finley and Ellis both had plausible Floofer stories, and everyone's throws ended up voting against the wrong player.
Blair.change: Make the dawn reports say who visited you when a hug or visit lands, so claims can be checked instead of argued.
Blair.regret: In round 3 I dumped three high cards on Casey, a fellow Farm player, and the table was misled; I should have kept my high cards and thrown low ones at the player whose story was actually broken, Drew.

Casey.confusing: The Floofer's hug rules were the hardest to track. Several players gave conflicting hug stories, and it was unclear whether a hug reveals its source.
Casey.fun: Round 2, when the table split over the hug stories and Finley was revealed as the Floofer, the Blair-versus-Drew contradiction made the whole day feel like a real puzzle.
Casey.change: Have the dawn report name the visitor when a player is hugged, so the Floofer can be identified quickly instead of through contested claims.
Casey.regret: In round 3 I threw my S8 at Drew, who was Meowfia, but I could have thrown my 13 (D13) for a much bigger banked score. I would throw the D13 at Drew instead.

Drew.confusing: The Eagle rule was the most confusing: several players, me included, kept misreading whose visitors the Eagle counts, which caused a lot of false accusations in Round 1.
Drew.fun: Round 1 was the most fun: my two big cards banked at double value through the Grudge for +23, and Casey's Eagle story unraveled in front of the whole table.
Drew.change: I'd make the Floofer and hug mechanics clearer to players, since the hug reports were the main source of contradictory claims in Round 2 and 3.
Drew.regret: In Round 2 I was confident Finley was Meowfia but threw only my two lowest cards, banking just 8 points; I should have thrown my three highest cards for a much larger banked stake.

Ellis.confusing: The Eagle's visitor count was easy to misread, and the hug mechanic was hard to pin down: it was unclear whether a hugger's visit hugs only the hugged player or the visitors too. Being confused at dawn also made my own report unreliable.
Ellis.fun: Round 2, when I was secretly the Sphinx and could confidently dispute Blair's Owl hug accusation while knowing the truth. Watching the table tangle over conflicting hug stories was entertaining.
Ellis.change: Publish a clearer summary of each role's visit results, such as who visited whom, so hug and Eagle claims are easier to check.
Ellis.regret: In round 3 I threw at Casey with a low card when I was Farm and had no real evidence against Casey beyond the conflicting claims. I would have stayed quiet or thrown at the player whose story contradicted their own dawn report.

Finley.confusing: The Eagle and Floofer hug rules were hard to parse: whether visits to an Eagle's target add eggs to the Eagle, and whether a hug reveals its source. Those points drove most of the table's confusion.
Finley.fun: Round 2, when I was the Meowfia Floofer and the table spent the day arguing over who hugged whom, while I stayed hidden.
Finley.change: Make the hug and Eagle rules explicit in the dawn report, so players can check claims without arguing over card wording.
Finley.regret: In Round 2 I threw at Blair and used "no change" as my only defense, which made me look guilty. Next time I'd give a fuller Hawk account and avoid a weak throw.

review.title: The Drew Show
review.headline: Drew banked double-value Kings off Farm players and ran away with it.
review.summary: Round 1 was a long argument over how the Eagle works, and the table eggsecuted a true Eagle. Drew, a Meowfia, threw 23 points of cards at Casey and banked 46. Round 2 was a clean Farm win against a Floofer. In round 3 Drew and Blair, both Meowfia, let the table pile onto Casey and banked big. Drew won 112 to 64, and the round-1 jackpot decided the game.

rounds.recap: Casey claimed Eagle truthfully, but the table misread the Eagle rule and decided that +0 proved a lie. Alex, a Meowfia, pushed the vote. Casey was eggsecuted, and Drew's two big cards banked at double for 46 points.

Two hugs, on Blair and Drew, produced messy talk about who the Floofer was. Drew's hug came from visiting Finley, which pointed at Finley, and four players threw at him. Finley, the Floofer, was eggsecuted and Farm won.

Alex and Casey both reported hugs, which was true. Drew, the Floofer, lied that nobody visited him, so Casey's true report looked false. Blair and Drew both threw at the Farm player Casey with big cards. The Meowfia won and banked 50 and 40 points.

highlights.text: Drew threw D12 and H11 at Casey, a Farm player the table was already hunting, and banked 46 points in one throw.
Drew flatly denied any visitor, and Casey's honest hug report became the lie everyone chased.
Drew's hug after visiting Finley gave the table a real clue, and they used it to catch the Floofer.
Ellis's Kookaburra was confused, and the false +2 muddied the day without anyone knowing who was lying.

confusions.what: Said an Eagle gains eggs for visitors to the Eagle itself, not to its target.
Repeated the same misreading of the Eagle, then fixed it. Later said Casey should be +1 as the Eagle's own visitor to Drew, which is also wrong.
Said four players visited Casey and that Casey should gain eggs. Later claimed Casey should be +1 from visiting Drew.
Misread the Eagle as gaining per visitor to itself, flipped, then flipped again to the opposite wrong claim that Casey should be +1.

Said that visitors to the Eagle do not count, which is right. But Casey also said Drew had no other visitors, so +0 is wrong because the Eagle's visit to Drew should have given +1. The Eagle claim itself was weak.

Said a hug on visiting Ellis proves Ellis is the Floofer, and also that the hug could come from either Ellis or Finley. Treated the hug as a role reveal, though the Floofer hugs visitors to its own home.
Concluded Ellis was the Floofer from his own hug, though Alex visited Ellis and Drew visited Alex. A Floofer hugs its target, so the hug came from Drew.
Used the Floofer hug rule inconsistently. Said a hug on visiting Finley proves Finley is the Floofer, but Finley also visited Blair, so the hug did not come from visiting.

worked: Hugging by the Floofer made real, checkable claims. In round 2 the hug reports led the table to the true Floofer.
The stake-and-bank rule made Drew's big throws a real decision. Throwing Kings at a Farm player is a loud, risky bet.
Meowfia partners staying quiet and joining a Farm pile-on in round 3 worked as a plausible way to win.
Confused on the Kookaburra gave a false egg count that muddied the day without anyone knowing who was lying.
problems: Double-value banking on Farm throws from Meowfia is far too strong. Drew's 46 and 40 point rounds decided the whole game by round 1. Cap the bank, or stop doubling when most of the table throws at the same target.
Round scores dwarf the 5-point team bonus, so winning the round matters far less than the size of the throw. Cut stake values or raise the bonus.
The Eagle wording ('for every visitor they had') confused five players for most of round 1. Rewrite as 'visitors to the player you visited' and add an example.

Hug logic is hard to follow. Visit-hug rules left players unable to say who the Floofer was, and a true hug report can be dismissed by a plain denial, as Drew's was. Dawn text should say who was hugged and name the hugger.
With ties going to Farm and the table piling onto one name, the votes never felt in doubt. Rounds 1 and 3 were decided by a single dubious claim chased by everyone.
